title: Femoral access landmark: inferior epigastric artery marks the inguinal ligament
vignette: A 63-year-old man undergoes coronary angiography via right common femoral artery access for evaluation of exertional chest pain. During the procedure, contrast is injected and an angiogram of the right pelvic and femoral vasculature is obtained. The arrow in the image indicates an artery that arises from the external iliac artery just proximal to the inguinal ligament and courses medially and superiorly along the anterior abdominal wall toward the umbilicus. Correctly identifying this vessel helps confirm that the arterial puncture was made below the inguinal ligament. Which of the following arteries is indicated by the arrow?

clues.text: arises from the external iliac artery just proximal to the inguinal ligament
clues.note: The last branch of the external iliac artery before it becomes the common femoral (at the inguinal ligament) is the INFERIOR EPIGASTRIC artery - a key angiographic landmark for the inguinal ligament.

clues.text: courses medially and superiorly along the anterior abdominal wall toward the umbilicus
clues.note: The inferior epigastric artery runs up the anterior abdominal wall (in the rectus sheath, forming the lateral umbilical fold) to anastomose with the superior epigastric artery.

clues.text: confirm that the arterial puncture was made below the inguinal ligament
clues.note: The inferior epigastric artery's origin marks the inguinal ligament: femoral punctures ABOVE it (into the external iliac) risk uncontrollable RETROPERITONEAL hemorrhage because that segment cannot be compressed against the femoral head.

whatMatters: The vessel arising from the EXTERNAL ILIAC artery just above the inguinal ligament, running toward the umbilicus, is the INFERIOR EPIGASTRIC ARTERY. Its origin marks the inguinal ligament and thus the safe zone for femoral puncture (below it, over the femoral head). Answer A.
strategy: Anchor on the described course: a branch of the external iliac artery, arising just above the inguinal ligament, ascending the anterior abdominal wall toward the umbilicus = inferior epigastric artery. Link it to vascular-access safety (punctures above the inferior epigastric origin = above inguinal ligament -> retroperitoneal bleed risk). Reject deep femoral/profunda (arises below the ligament, supplies thigh), obturator (from internal iliac, into medial thigh), lateral femoral circumflex (from deep femoral), superficial epigastric (from femoral, small/subcutaneous), and internal pudendal (from internal iliac, to perineum).

eliminations.label: Deep femoral (profunda femoris) - below the ligament, into the thigh
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the largest branch of the femoral artery, arising BELOW the inguinal ligament to supply the thigh. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it does not ascend the abdominal wall toward the umbilicus and does not mark the inguinal ligament. ✅ Correct if: a large thigh-supplying branch of the common femoral artery.

eliminations.label: Obturator artery - from internal iliac, into medial thigh
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: usually a branch of the internal iliac artery passing through the obturator canal to the medial thigh. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it neither arises from the external iliac nor runs toward the umbilicus. ✅ Correct if: vessel through the obturator foramen to adductors.

eliminations.label: Lateral femoral circumflex - from deep femoral, around the femur
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a branch of the deep femoral artery that wraps laterally around the femoral neck. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is a thigh vessel below the ligament, not an abdominal-wall landmark. ✅ Correct if: branch encircling the proximal femur.

eliminations.label: Superficial epigastric - from femoral, subcutaneous
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a small superficial branch of the femoral artery running subcutaneously toward the umbilicus. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it arises BELOW the inguinal ligament from the femoral artery and is small/subcutaneous, not the deep external-iliac branch used as the ligament landmark. ✅ Correct if: small superficial abdominal-wall vessel from the femoral artery.

eliminations.label: Internal pudendal - from internal iliac, to perineum
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a branch of the internal iliac artery supplying the perineum and external genitalia. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: wrong parent vessel and wrong territory; it does not ascend toward the umbilicus. ✅ Correct if: perineal/genital arterial supply.

reasoning: The vessel arises from the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament
It ascends the anterior abdominal wall toward the umbilicus
That course defines the inferior epigastric artery (the ligament landmark)
mechanism: The EXTERNAL ILIAC artery gives off two branches just before it passes under the inguinal ligament to become the common femoral artery: the INFERIOR EPIGASTRIC artery and the deep circumflex iliac artery. The inferior epigastric artery courses MEDIALLY and SUPERIORLY along the anterior abdominal wall (raising the lateral umbilical fold and entering the rectus sheath) to anastomose with the superior epigastric artery near the umbilicus. Because it originates at the level of the inguinal ligament, it is the key ANGIOGRAPHIC LANDMARK for safe femoral arterial access: the ideal puncture is BELOW the inferior epigastric origin (i.e., below the inguinal ligament, over the femoral head, where the artery can be compressed). A puncture ABOVE this point enters the external iliac artery within the retroperitoneum, where bleeding cannot be tamponaded by external compression and can cause a life-threatening RETROPERITONEAL HEMORRHAGE. The distractors are either branches that arise below the ligament from the femoral/deep femoral (profunda femoris, lateral femoral circumflex, superficial epigastric) or branches of the internal iliac (obturator, internal pudendal) - none of which mark the inguinal ligament.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid / anatomy: external iliac artery -> inferior epigastric + deep circumflex iliac before becoming common femoral; inferior epigastric ascends abdominal wall (lateral umbilical fold); femoral access landmark; high puncture -> retroperitoneal bleed.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Branch of external iliac just above the inguinal ligament, running to the umbilicus = inferior epigastric artery.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on inferior epigastric artery, external iliac, inguinal ligament, retroperitoneal hemorrhage, or femoral access? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Profunda/lateral circumflex/superficial epigastric arise below the ligament; obturator/internal pudendal come off the internal iliac.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.text: Angiogram (stem image): the arrow marks a vessel from the external iliac ascending toward the umbilicus = inferior epigastric; it flags the inguinal-ligament level for safe puncture.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: inferior epigastric artery = last external-iliac branch before the inguinal ligament; landmark for safe femoral puncture (below it = over femoral head).

keywords.front: Artery arising from external iliac just above inguinal ligament
Femoral puncture ABOVE inguinal ligament risk
Inferior epigastric forms which peritoneal fold

keywords.back: Common femoral artery over the femoral head (below the ligament)

firstAid.detail: Anatomy: branch of external iliac; abdominal-wall course; femoral-access landmark.
Vascular access > high femoral puncture (above inferior epigastric) -> non-compressible bleed.
Anatomy > profunda femoris, obturator, circumflex, pudendal parent vessels.

memoryHook: Aim BELOW the inferior epigastric - it's the 'do-not-cross' line at the inguinal ligament; puncture above it and blood hides in the retroperitoneum where no hand can press.
